messages.author: 50b36e864fb52ac0
messages.subject: Help with modified gm.prcomp
parts:
Hello all! I am trying to do something a bit unconventional with gm.prcomp. I need to make a morphospace with 41 taxa, and then reconstruct ancestral characters in a phylogeny of only 26 of those 41 taxa. I am trying to modify the gm.prcomp function to do this, but so far it has proven to be beyond my limited R programming skills.

I created a modified gm.prcomp function called gm.prcomp.mod. In that function I commented the part that stops the function if the number of taxa are different in the phylogeny and data matrix.

 #if (N != n)
 #  stop("Number of taxa in data matrix and tree are not equal.\n",
 #       call. = FALSE)

Trying to use this modified function to do a regular ancestral state reconstruction works fine, so I'm confident the function still works.
When I try to do what I intend to do with the modified function (morphospace built with 41 taxa, ancestral state reconstruction in phylogeny with only 26 taxa), I get the following error:

Error in C[rownames(x), rownames(x)] : subscript out of bounds

Which is expected I guess, but I haven't been able to find a solution to this problem. Any help in this matter would be greatly appreciated.



--
Vicente Muñoz Walther
Ph.D.(c)
Laboratorio de Ontogenia y Filogenia
Las Palmeras 3425
Universidad de Chile

messages.author: f16866fc42d43e64
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with modified gm.prcomp
parts:
Vicente,

not sure what the biological meaning of this morphospace would be, but it would be easier if you first calculate the PCA with the taxa included in your phylogeny, and then project the shapes of those species for which the phylogenetic position is unknown on the eigenvectors of that PCA to visualize their position. Otherwise you will never be able to match the data with shape data (41) with those on the phylogeny (26), which is what that line of code does (C being the phylogenetic covariance matrix, with dimensions as many as the tips of your tree).

Antigoni

parts:
Hi, thanks for the response!
Its not that the phylogenetic position of the 15 taxa I excluded from the phylogenetic tree are unknown. Those 15 taxa are in fact duplicates of taxa already in the tree, but with a different landmarking hypothesis.
Let me explain to try to make sense to this.
I have 11 taxa with unambiguous landmarking and 15 taxa in which the landmarking is ambiguous between two hypothesis, we'll call them H1 and H2. My goal is to find out which of the two landmarking hypothesis is more likely, based on the phylogenetic relationship between the 15 ambiguous taxa and the 11 unambiguous taxa. Since two different morphospaces cannot be compared (as I understand it), I thought about creating a morphospace including the 11 unambiguous taxa and the 15 ambiguous taxa with both hypothesis, for a total of 41 taxa (11 unambiguous, 15 ambiguous with H1 and 15 ambiguous with H2).
With this in mind, I thought of doing an ancestral state reconstruction for both hypothesis, seeing the rate of morphological change along the backbone of each phylogeny. Both phylogenies would be identical in topology and branch length, but would differ in that one would include the ambiguous taxa landmarked with H1 (taxa1H1, taxa2H1, taxa3H1, ...etc.) and the other would include the ambiguous taxa landmarked with H2 (taxa1H2, taxa2H2, taxa3H2, ... etc.). My thought is that the phylogeny that implies a larger rate of morphological change is less likely.
Any help in this matter would be tremendously appreciated.

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with modified gm.prcomp
parts:
Vicente,

I believe you cannot attempt to do what you intend to do without contriving a different phylogeny, so I would recommend abandoning this approach.  Rather, if you have 15 taxa with alternative landmark configurations, my recommendation would be to create two data sets: one with the 11 unambiguous taxa and H1 version of the 15 ambiguous taxa and one with the 11 unambiguous taxa and the H2 version.  You assert that one should be more likely based on phylogenetic relationships, which implies for me that it would be the one with greater phylogenetic signal, which you can compute on each set.

This advice assumes that it makes sense to have alternative landmarking hypotheses that are somehow convergent for the 11 taxa (they would have the same configurations by either hypothesis).  I cannot imagine how this is the case.  If it is not the case, assuming there is a common morphospace for alternative landmark configurations might be a grave mistake.  The math will not care as long as the number of landmarks is consistent but trying to make sense of and compare patterns in this space might not be wise.  If you insist on combining 11, 15, and 15 landmark configurations to create a morphospace, please realize that you cannot use a phylogeny that does not have 41 taxa.  But you can make two separate ordination plots with 26 taxa each, project the ancestral states into each, and see which seems to align bet with the first component (assuming you are doing a phylogenetically aligned component analysis).

I hope that makes sense.

Best,
Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with modified gm.prcomp
parts: Hi Vicente,

" ... my recommendation would be to create two data sets: one with the 11 unambiguous taxa and H1 version of the 15 ambiguous taxa and one with the 11 unambiguous taxa and the H2 version.  You assert that one should be more likely based on phylogenetic relationships, which implies for me that it would be the one with greater phylogenetic signal, which you can compute on each set."

With this in mind, can the phylogenetic signals resulting from these two datasets be compared with one another? I have not worked with phylogenetic signal before, so there is a lot I am not quite familiar with.

Yes, they can be compared.  You can obtain Z-scores from analyses and compare them statistically in a two-sample test or just compare them, qualitatively.  In fact, we just published an article related to this (found here or here).

" But you can make two separate ordination plots with 26 taxa each, project the ancestral states into each, and see which seems to align bet with the first component (assuming you are doing a phylogenetically aligned component analysis)."

My intuition tells that this will generate two different morphospaces, and as I understand it, different morphospaces cannot be compared with one another. Is that not the case? Still, I will look into this as a solution to my problem.

Well, kind of no and yes.  There is a shape space for the number of landmarks you use, but if landmarks are arranged differently in your configurations (H1 and H2), then there would be clusters of (taxon) shapes separated distinctly in that space, and the reference (center of an ordination) would probably make little biological sense.  You would be forced to change your focus to make sense of any pattern in each cluster of the points.  This would mean performing separate ordinations within the clusters.  Here is an example.

> data(plethspecies) 
> 
> coords1 <- coords2 <- plethspecies$land
> coords2 <- coords2[c(2, 1, 3:11),,] # switch lm 1 and 2
> 
> list1 <- lapply(1:9, function(x) coords1[,, x])
> list2 <- lapply(1:9, function(x) coords2[,, x])
> 
> coords <- simplify2array(c(list1, list2)) # combine configuration sets
> 
> Y.gpa <- gpagen(coords)    #GPA-alignment
> plot(gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords))


Now, we could zero in on each cluster and try to make sense of them.  Let’s do this with the following code.

> Y <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)$x
> rownames(Y) <- c(dimnames(coords1)[[3]], dimnames(coords2)[[3]])
> par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
> PCA1 <- gm.prcomp(Y[1:9, ], phy = plethspecies$phy)
> PCA2 <- gm.prcomp(Y[10:18, ], phy = plethspecies$phy)
> plot(PCA1, phylo = TRUE)
> plot(PCA2, phylo = TRUE)


As you can see, zeroing in on the two clusters produced the same plots, arbitrary rotation of PCs, notwithstanding.  What if we had just done PCA on the different sets, separately?

> PCA1 <- gm.prcomp(coords1, phy = plethspecies$phy)
> PCA2 <- gm.prcomp(coords2, phy = plethspecies$phy)
> plot(PCA1, phylo = TRUE)
> plot(PCA2, phylo = TRUE)

So the same result.  What this example shows is creating a single morphospace (first plot) does not do anything but create clusters of points that need to be viewed separately to understand how ancestral character states are dispersed.  Whether one wishes to acknowledge one or two separate morphospaces does not matter.  One would still have to look at a plot of N points for N taxa and ad to that plot the N - 1 ancestral states.  Contriving a 2N phylogeny with 2N - 1 ancestral states would not help in anyway that I can see. Performing PCA twice just changes the reference to be in the center of the cluster of points, but if it makes you feel better, you could compare the dispersion of points and think of them coming from different portions of the same morphospace.

Best,
Mike

Thank you so much for the help. Any further help would be greatly appreciated.
